contributions.headingText: Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal neoplasm with smooth muscle differentiation.

8890/3 Leiomyosarcoma, NOS

8890/3 Superficial leiomyosarcoma

8890/3 Deep leiomyosarcoma

Genitourinary tract sarcomas are rare, accounting for 1–2% of all genitourinary malignancies {32094047; 33169456}, and leiomyosarcoma is the most common histological type {33169456}. About half to three quarters of all soft tissue leiomyosarcomas arise in the retroperitoneum, with a smaller number occurring in the peritoneal cavity and pelvis {32446433; 28287938}. Primary genitourinary sites include the bladder {30384363; 25027684; 20154594}, prostate {23250042; 29297486; 26640482; 19043598}, and kidney; in this last site, tumours may arise from the renal capsule, renal parenchyma, smooth muscle cells of the intrarenal blood vessels, main renal vein, or renal pelvis {28265233; 32491531; 26860013}. Primary leiomyosarcomas of the paratesticular tissue {17070247; 11688573; 30044590} are very uncommon and may arise from the epididymis {22154176}, scrotum {21686870}, or spermatic cord {24885500; 30981071}. Small series and individual cases of penile leiomyosarcomas have been reported {16927639; 29019335; 18005170; 14707873}, most of which are of vascular origin and classified as either superficial or deep-seated.

Patients with leiomyosarcoma typically present with a mass discovered at imaging for abdominal fullness or pain {32446433}. Tumours are usually clinically silent or cause mild symptoms until they involve vital organs {28287938}. Back pain, abdominal distention, and changes in bladder or bowel habits are due to mass effect or organ involvement. Patients with urinary bladder leiomyosarcoma commonly present with gross haematuria, urinary frequency, and dysuria {12809885}. Penile leiomyosarcomas may cause dysuria and difficulty voiding {14707873}.

Leiomyosarcoma is one of the most common soft tissue sarcomas {17070247}, accounting for 5–10% of cases. They commonly affect middle-aged and older adults (peak incidence occurs in the seventh decade), with a female predominance (M:F ratio: 2:3) {32446433}. Leiomyosarcoma is the most common sarcoma of the adult kidney and accounts for 50–60% of all renal sarcomas. Primary sarcomas of the paratesticular tissue {17070247; 11688573} are very uncommon.

Leiomyosarcomas are large, well-circumscribed, white to grey, soft to firm, fleshy, encapsulated masses; their cut surface may have a whorled appearance. Large tumours frequently exhibit haemorrhage, necrosis, or cystic changes {32446433}.

Leiomyosarcomas are typically composed of elongated spindle cells with blunt-ended nuclei arranged in intersecting fascicles. Well-differentiated tumours contain spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and mild cytological atypia; epithelioid cells may be seen admixed with spindle cells. Poorly differentiated neoplasms demonstrate nuclear pleomorphism, increased mitotic activity, or necrosis {32446433}. Adult genitourinary sarcomas have been subdivided into low-grade and high-grade {17070247; 23601444; 32094047}. In the urinary bladder, the distinction has been based on mitotic activity (≥ 1 mitosis/mm2), nuclear atypia (mild to moderate), and tumour necrosis (< 25%) {11859200}. High-grade leiomyosarcomas of the bladder appear to behave more aggressively than low-grade tumours {11859200}. Most leiomyosarcomas arising in the genitourinary tract are high-grade {28459169; 23601444}, with the exception of paratesticular tumours.

Leiomyosarcoma cells are typically positive for α-SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon, and calponin, at least focally; they are negative for S100. In the differential diagnosis, rare cases of gastrointestinal stromal tumours have to be considered, especially in the prostate.
Essential: nuclear atypia, pleomorphism, ≥ 1 mitosis/mm2, and/or necrosis; immunoreactivity for SMA and desmin.

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system for soft tissue sarcoma is the most widely used system for staging leiomyosarcoma. It combines primary tumour size, lymph node involvement, presence of metastasis, sarcoma type and grade, and tumour depth {28287938}.

Tumour size, extent of local invasion (depth), surgical margin/resectability, histological grade, and presence of metastatic disease are the most important prognostic factors {17070247}. Surgical resection with negative margins remains the only potential curative treatment {11882765; 32446433; 33169456}. Primary renal sarcomas are highly aggressive neoplasms with a poor prognosis {21071373}. Patients with sarcomas of the bladder, prostate, and kidney have worse survival than those with paratesticular and scrotal sarcomas {32094047; 15774243}. The most common sites of metastases are the liver and lung. Superficial leiomyosarcomas of the penis are usually low-grade, with limited capacity for distant metastasis. However, deep-seated tumours often show aggressive behaviour and are associated with a poor prognosis {23949127; 15992427; 14707873}.
